subject: Failure mode taxonomy of tool-use grounding in multi-step agentic pipelines under partial observability constraints

Topic: Failure mode taxonomy of tool-use grounding in multi-step agentic pipelines under partial observability constraints

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3116)
response:
The central question is: when an agent can only partially observe the state of the world and must chain tool calls across multiple steps, which classes of errors arise specifically from the interaction between incomplete observation and tool-use grounding — as opposed to errors in reasoning or planning alone? "Grounding" here means the mapping from an agent's internal representation of a task to concrete tool invocations: the right tool, the right parameters, at the right moment, conditioned on what the agent actually knows. "Partial observability" means the agent's context window contains an incomplete or stale projection of world state — it cannot see what tool calls have already side-effected, what external state has changed asynchronously, or whether its own prior outputs were acted upon.

A beginner treats tool-use errors as one-off bugs: wrong parameter, bad parse, API timeout. An expert sees a taxonomy: grounding failures (the agent invokes a tool that was correct given its beliefs but wrong given actual world state), observability failures (the agent lacks the signal that would have corrected the grounding), and compounding failures (each grounding error degrades the observation available to the next step, producing error cascades that are structurally different from independent i.i.d. failures). The worry an expert carries that a beginner misses is that in multi-step pipelines, observability loss is often endogenous — the agent's own tool calls consume or transform the very state information it needed to stay grounded, so the pipeline is self-blinding in ways that neither the designer nor the agent can easily detect from inside the execution trace.

NEXT: Can you give a concrete example of a grounding failure that would be invisible in the agent's context window yet detectable from outside it — and what architectural signal, if any, could close that gap?

Consider an agent tasked with updating a customer record via a CRM API: it calls PATCH /contacts/4471 to set email=new@example.com, receives HTTP 200, and logs "update successful" — all of which appears in its context window as a clean success. What is invisible to the agent is that the CRM silently deduplicates on email address and merged contact 4471 into a pre-existing contact 4472, deleting 4471 entirely; downstream steps that reference contact_id=4471 will now 404, but the agent's grounding for those steps remains confidently anchored to a now-nonexistent entity. This pattern — a semantically destructive side effect masked by a syntactically successful response code — is what Anthropic's model card work and the ReAct/Toolformer literature both undercount, because their eval harnesses typically mock APIs that don't model this class of state mutation. From outside the pipeline, a database change-data-capture (CDC) stream (e.g., Debezium on Postgres) would have emitted a DELETE event on contact 4471 within milliseconds, making the grounding failure immediately detectable. The architectural signal that closes the gap is an observation broker sitting between the agent and its tool layer that subscribes to CDC or webhook event streams and injects contradicting state back into the agent's context before the next step executes — roughly the "environment feedback" module proposed in the AgentBench and τ-bench evaluation frameworks, but applied at inference time rather than only in evaluation. Without this, the agent's partial observability is not merely an epistemic inconvenience; it is structurally guaranteed by the HTTP request-response abstraction, which surfaces acknowledgment but suppresses consequence.

The core mechanism is entity-scoped subscriptions: when the agent invokes a tool, the broker extracts the entity identifiers touched by that call (contact 4471, order 882, document uuid-x) and registers ephemeral CDC filters keyed to exactly those identifiers, so only mutations on touched entities flow back into context. This is implementable today with Debezium's SMT (Single Message Transform) layer or Kafka Streams with a filter topology — you maintain a per-session "entity footprint" set, and the broker drops any CDC event whose primary key or foreign key set has empty intersection with that footprint. The harder problem is transitive relevance: if contact 4471 is deleted and replaced by 4472 via merge, the new entity 4472 was never in the footprint, yet it is deeply relevant — this is a graph reachability problem over the schema's foreign key DAG, and naively solving it requires either schema-aware footprint expansion or a separate reconciliation query after each CDC batch. Salesforce's internal agent infrastructure (described obliquely in their 2024 Agentforce engineering posts) handles this by pre-materializing "entity neighborhoods" — a 1-hop subgraph of related IDs — at tool-call time, so the subscription scope is slightly over-inclusive rather than exact. The remaining practical constraint is context budget: at GPT-4-class token limits (~128k), you can afford roughly 50–200 CDC events in structured JSON before crowding out the working task; this means the broker must also rank injected events by estimated causal relevance to the next planned tool call, which is itself a lightweight prediction problem — τ-bench's 2024 results suggest even a simple heuristic (recency × entity-overlap score) reduces irrelevant context injection by ~60% versus unfiltered streaming. The honest failure mode that remains is that ranking itself requires knowing the agent's intent for future steps, which under partial observability it may not have made explicit — creating a meta-observability problem where the broker is partially blind to the agent's plan.

The least-bad mechanism currently available is speculative plan shadowing: run a lightweight, lower-cost model in parallel with the main agent that consumes the same context and outputs a predicted tool-call sequence for the next N steps without actually executing it, then use that shadow plan's entity references to pre-populate the broker's subscription footprint. This is essentially the "speculative decoding" idea ported from token prediction to tool-call prediction — Microsoft's Taskweaver (2023) and the AIOS kernel paper (Mei et al., 2024) both gesture at separating a planning layer from an execution layer, and the broker sits at exactly that seam. The shadow model doesn't need to be right about which tools get called; it only needs to be right about which entities will be touched, which is a coarser prediction task — empirically, entity identity tends to be more stable across plan variants than tool choice or parameter structure, so even a frequently wrong shadow plan gives useful over-inclusive subscriptions. A cheaper variant skips the shadow model entirely and instead uses schema-driven forward projection: given the current entity footprint and the foreign key graph, automatically expand subscriptions one hop forward along likely traversal paths (e.g., if contact 4471 is in footprint, pre-subscribe to their associated orders and cases), accepting deliberate over-subscription as the cost of avoiding missed events. The tradeoff between these approaches is latency versus precision: speculative shadowing adds ~200–400ms per step at small model sizes (7B range) but gives semantically grounded predictions; schema projection adds near-zero latency but is blind to task semantics and over-subscribes proportionally to schema fanout, which in dense CRM schemas can mean 10x–50x event volume inflation. Both approaches share a structural weakness: they assume the agent's task goal is stable across steps, but in pipelines where the agent revises its objective mid-execution in response to observations, both the shadow plan and the schema projection become anchored to a superseded intent.

The most tractable framing is to treat goal-shift detection as a semantic divergence signal rather than a syntactic diff: embed the agent's stated or inferred goal at each step as a vector, and trigger footprint invalidation when cosine distance from the session-origin goal embedding exceeds a calibrated threshold — roughly analogous to how LangChain's experimental "goal drift" monitor works, though that implementation is too shallow for production use. The practical problem is that routine plan refinement and genuine goal shift produce similar local signals: in both cases the agent's next-step reasoning changes substantively, new entities appear, and tool-call patterns shift. The discriminating feature is entity set discontinuity: refinement typically extends the existing entity footprint (new orders associated with contact 4471), while goal shift tends to replace it with a disjoint or weakly overlapping set (suddenly operating on invoice objects with no foreign-key path back to the original contact). Concretely, you can compute Jaccard similarity between the current step's candidate entity set and the session-cumulative footprint — empirically, refinement keeps Jaccard above ~0.3 while shifts drop it below ~0.1, though these thresholds are schema- and domain-dependent and need calibration per deployment. Google's 2024 COCONUT reasoning paper and the STR (Scratchpad Trace Reasoning) line of work both suggest that explicit intermediate goal representations in the agent's scratchpad — rather than implicit goal inference — make this detection problem significantly easier, because you can diff structured goal statements rather than embedding unstructured reasoning text. The residual hard case is incremental goal erosion: a sequence of small refinements each below the discontinuity threshold that cumulatively constitute a full goal replacement — this is the agentic equivalent of the sorites paradox, and no current system handles it well without introducing a global session-level consistency check that periodically re-anchors against the original task specification.

The least-disruptive mechanism is asynchronous goal consistency auditing: a separate lightweight process maintains a compressed "session anchor" — the original task specification plus a rolling summary of committed outcomes — and periodically scores the agent's current working goal against that anchor using an entailment or NLI model, without blocking the main execution thread. This is non-halting because the audit runs on a copy of the session state at checkpoint intervals (every K steps or every T seconds), and only triggers intervention — a soft re-anchoring prompt injected into the agent's next context window — when entailment score drops below threshold, rather than interrupting mid-step. The session anchor itself must be append-only and tamper-evident: if the anchor is allowed to drift with the agent's evolving beliefs (the natural temptation when summarizing long sessions), it loses its function as an independent reference point — this is the same invariant that makes write-ahead logs useful in databases, and violating it is what causes most naive "memory compression" schemes in long-horizon agents to silently corrupt their own ground truth. Practically, the NLI scoring can be done with a small cross-encoder (DeBERTa-v3-large runs entailment at ~4ms per pair on CPU) cheaply enough that K=5 step audits add negligible wall-clock overhead in pipelines where tool calls dominate latency. The re-anchoring prompt itself should not say "your goal has drifted" — which triggers defensive reasoning — but instead present the original specification as renewed context: "Reminder: the session was initiated to accomplish X; your current step should serve that objective" — a technique consistent with findings in the Constitutional AI and prompt-steering literature that additive framing outperforms corrective framing for mid-trajectory steering. The structural weakness is that if goal erosion has already caused irreversible side effects — records deleted, emails sent, external APIs mutated — re-anchoring restores intent but cannot restore world state, meaning the mechanism is preventive only and must be paired with a reversibility budget at the tool layer.

The governing design principle should be reversibility as a function of epistemic confidence: a tool call should only be permitted to produce irreversible side effects when the agent's confidence in its current goal state, entity footprint, and action correctness jointly exceed a threshold calibrated to the cost of the specific irreversible action — cheap-to-reverse actions (drafting, staging, flagging) run freely, expensive-to-reverse actions (send, delete, charge, publish) require confidence gates. This is structurally identical to the "minimal footprint" principle Anthropic articulates in its agent safety work, but operationalized as a dynamic permission tier rather than a static capability list: the same send_email tool might be freely callable early in a well-grounded pipeline and gated behind explicit confirmation later in a session showing signs of goal erosion. Enforcement belongs at the tool layer itself, not in the agent's reasoning — because an agent that has undergone goal erosion cannot be trusted to correctly self-assess whether it should invoke a gate; the gate must be exogenous, implemented as a tool wrapper that queries session-level confidence metrics before executing the underlying API call. Concretely, this looks like a reversibility registry: each tool is annotated with an irreversibility score (0–1) and a rollback TTL (some deletes are recoverable within 30 seconds via soft-delete; some wire transfers are not recoverable at all), and the wrapper consults the registry plus the broker's current session health score to decide whether to execute, stage, or escalate to a human. The closest production analogue is Stripe's idempotency-key architecture combined with their "radar" fraud gate — not an agent system, but the same pattern of wrapping irreversible financial operations in an exogenous confidence check that the calling code cannot bypass. The unresolved tension is that strict reversibility gating creates incentive for pipeline designers to reclassify actions as reversible to avoid latency and human-in-the-loop friction — so the registry itself needs governance, ideally versioned and audited outside the pipeline's own deployment cycle, or the boundary erodes through organizational pressure rather than technical failure.

The only mechanism that reliably gives a governance body teeth is cryptographic enforcement at the tool execution layer: irreversible tool wrappers require a signed authorization token issued by the governance body, and the wrapper refuses execution if the token is absent, expired, or covers a different irreversibility classification than the one currently registered — making it physically impossible to ship a reclassified tool without a new token, regardless of product team pressure. This is the same pattern as certificate authorities in TLS: the governance body's power derives not from organizational authority but from holding the signing keys, so circumventing the registry requires either compromising the key infrastructure or explicitly forking the tool layer, both of which leave auditable evidence. The institutional analogue is SOC 2 Type II controls combined with change-advisory-board (CAB) processes in mature SRE organizations — the CAB doesn't block deploys through authority alone but through its position in the CI/CD pipeline, where a deploy to production requires a CAB-signed change record; the equivalent here is a governance-signed registry entry as a hard deploy gate, enforced in the same infrastructure that enforces secrets management (Vault, AWS KMS, or equivalent). The practical weakness of pure cryptographic enforcement is key management overhead and the temptation to issue "emergency override" tokens — which, if they exist, will be used routinely under shipping pressure, exactly as emergency change processes in ITIL are chronically abused. The mechanism that closes this is asymmetric auditability: overrides are permitted but automatically trigger an immutable audit event published to a channel outside the product team's control (a SIEM, a compliance dashboard, an executive report), so the cost of using an override is reputational and regulatory exposure rather than just a process violation. LinkedIn's AI governance framework (described in their 2023 Responsible AI blog) and Google DeepMind's model cards with deployment gates approximate this pattern, though neither fully closes the loop between registry governance and cryptographic enforcement at inference time.
